key_insight: Greater white matter hyperintensity (WMH) burden was more strongly associated with poorer verbal memory in non-Hispanic African American than non-Hispanic White older adults in two of three cohorts, with location-specific differences.
clinical_relevance: Spatially resolved WMH mapping may help researchers characterize early vascular contributions to cognitive aging, but these findings do not establish a clinical decision tool.
method: Analyzed 5,187 cognitively unimpaired older adults across three independent cohorts.
Mapped WMH by white matter depth and brain lobe using cross-sectional, longitudinal and machine learning analyses.
Evaluated associations after adjustment for cohort-specific biomarkers, vascular risks, structural imaging measures and APOE genotype.
evidence_signal: Group differences appeared in EHBS and a 34-center cohort but were not detected in the third cohort; baseline frontal juxtacortical WMH also showed a stronger association with subsequent AD-signature cortical thinning in African American participants in EHBS.
watch_item: Observational associations and inconsistent replication across cohorts limit causal interpretation; racial categories should not be treated as biological explanations.
paper_title: Spatially localized racial differences in the association between white matter hyperintensities and verbal memory in cognitively unimpaired adults
